prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
When you commit in Git, nothing is stored as a diff or a changeset. Everything lives in the .git directory as a simple key-value store, where the key is a SHA-1 hash (newer repositories can use SHA-256) and the value is a compressed object. Git has only four kinds of object, and understanding three of them, blobs, trees and commits, plus the small files called refs that point at them, explains most of what Git does.

The simplest object is the blob, which holds the raw contents of one file and nothing else. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp. Git prepends a short header giving the object type and byte length, hashes the header and contents together, and writes the result, compressed with zlib, to a path under .git/objects. The first two hex digits of the hash become a directory name and the remaining digits become the filename. Because the hash is computed from the content alone, two files with identical contents, even in different directories or at different points in history, share a single blob. This is also why renaming a file costs almost nothing in storage terms, since the content is already there.

Since blobs carry no names, something else must record which blob belongs to which path, and that is the job of the tree. A tree object represents one directory. It is a list of entries, and each entry holds a file mode, a name, and the hash of either a blob or another tree. The mode distinguishes a regular file from an executable, a symbolic link or a subdirectory. A directory containing a subdirectory is therefore a tree whose entries include the hash of a second tree, and so on down the hierarchy. The tree for the top-level directory of your project is the root of a complete snapshot, because following its entries recursively reaches every file as it existed at that moment. Like blobs, trees are named by the hash of their contents, so if you change one file deep in the project, only the blob for that file and the trees on the path from it up to the root need to be created. Every untouched sibling file and directory keeps its existing hash and is simply referenced again.

A commit object ties a snapshot to a point in history. It is a small text record containing the hash of the root tree, the hashes of zero or more parent commits, an author line and a committer line, each with a name, email address and timestamp, followed by a blank line and your commit message. The first commit in a repository has no parent, an ordinary commit has one, and a merge commit has two or more. These parent pointers are what turn a pile of snapshots into a history, and they run backwards in time, so each commit knows where it came from but nothing knows what comes after it. Because the commit's own hash is computed from all of these fields, including the parent hashes and the tree hash, changing anything about a past commit produces a different hash. That change then ripples through every descendant, which is why rewriting history with a rebase gives you new commits rather than editing the old ones.

The commit's hash is the only name Git really has for it, and nobody wants to type forty hexadecimal characters, so Git adds refs. A ref is just a file whose content is a hash. Your local branches live as files under .git/refs/heads, so the file named main there holds the hash of the commit at the tip of that branch. Tags live under .git/refs/tags, and remote-tracking branches such as origin/main live under .git/refs/remotes. Creating a branch therefore amounts to writing forty characters into a new file, which explains why branching in Git is so cheap. When you make a new commit, Git writes the new objects, sets the new commit's parent to the current tip, and then updates the branch file to point at the new commit. Nothing else changes.

One further file, .git/HEAD, tells Git where you currently are. Normally it contains a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, which is a symbolic reference meaning that HEAD follows whichever commit the main branch points to. When you check out a specific commit instead of a branch, HEAD holds a raw hash directly, and this is the state Git calls detached. Commits made in that state are not reachable from any branch, so they are eventually eligible for garbage collection unless you give them a branch name.

You can see all of this for yourself. The command git cat-file -p followed by a hash prints the contents of any object, and git cat-file -t prints its type. Running it on HEAD shows a commit, running it on the tree hash inside that commit shows the directory listing, and running it on a blob hash shows your file. Over time Git also packs many loose objects into compact packfiles that store similar objects as deltas, but that is only a storage optimization. Conceptually, a commit is always a pointer to a full tree of blobs, plus a message and a link to its parents.
